displayQuote: Failure is an event, not a person

meta.title: Who really said "Failure is an event, not a person"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Yes — Zig Ziglar. Wikiquote documents it in See You at the Top (revised 2000 edition) as “failure is an event, it is not a person — yesterday ended last night.”
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Failure is an event, not a person'?
meta.ogDescription: Genuinely Ziglar. Wikiquote records the full sentence in See You at the Top (Pelican; revised 2000 edition); the short one-liner is the form he printed in his own later books.

answer.label: Written by
answer.authorDates: 1926–2012 · American salesman, motivational speaker and author
answer.sourceLine: This one is genuinely his. It belongs to Ziglar’s first book, See You at the Top (Pelican Publishing, first published 1975), where Wikiquote documents the fuller form “failure is an event, it is not a person — yesterday ended last night” in the revised 2000 edition; the tightened one-liner everyone shares is also his, printed verbatim in books he wrote himself.

source.heading: The source

docMeta.dd: Revised 25th-anniversary edition, Pelican, 2000 — the edition Wikiquote cites

source.excerpt: The usual devastating put-downs imply that a person is basically bad, rather than that he is a person who sometimes does bad things. Obviously, there is a vast difference between a “bad” person and a person who does something bad. Besides, failure is an event, it is not a person — yesterday ended last night.
trail: Quote Investigator has no article on the phrase ↗ — its search returns nothing — so there is no specialist finding to defer to, and the question falls to the printed record.

Wikiquote’s sourced section ↗ files the sentence under See You at the Top — specifically under its heading for the revised 2000 edition — in the full form “failure is an event, it is not a person — yesterday ended last night,” listing the short popular wording as a variant.

Full-text search of scanned books returns the surrounding put-downs sentence inside three digitized Pelican printings of the book ↗ — so that framing paragraph is in the 1970s–90s text. The failure sentence itself is not: it is documented in the revised 2000 edition, which is the printing Wikiquote cites.
The exact short wording is present in books Ziglar wrote himself ↗, so the popular form is his own tightening rather than a stranger’s paraphrase.
source.cutTag: From the chapter on self-image · revised 2000 edition
source.excerptNote: Both forms are Ziglar’s, and the printed record does not settle which came first. Wikiquote documents this fuller wording in the revised 2000 edition; the tightened “failure is an event, not a person” appears word for word in his own Success for Dummies, You Can Reach the Top, Born to Win and Inspiration: 365 Days a Year. The digitized 1977, 1979 and 1991 Pelican printings carry the put-downs paragraph but not the failure sentence.

author.name: Zig Ziglar
author.heading: Who was Zig Ziglar?
author.metaLine: 1926–2012 · American salesman, motivational speaker and author of See You at the Top
author.bio: Hilary Hinton “Zig” Ziglar was born in Coffee County, Alabama, and started selling WearEver cookware door to door in 1947 — a job that became the raw material for four decades of speaking. He co-founded American Salesmasters in 1963 and established Ziglar, Inc. in 1977, writing more than thirty books along the way. His signature move was rhetorical rather than tactical: separating what a person did from what a person is, which is exactly the work this sentence does.

cite.sourceCitation: Zig Ziglar, See You at the Top (Gretna, LA: Pelican Publishing Company, first published 1975). Surrounding paragraph confirmed by full-text search of the digitized Pelican printings (1977, 1979 and 1991) held by the Internet Archive; the quoted sentence is cited to See You at the Top, revised 25th-anniversary edition (Pelican, 2000), per Wikiquote. The book was originally issued under the title Biscuits, Fleas, and Pump Handles.

misattribution.heading: What goes wrong with this one
misattribution.intro: The attribution is right — unusually, for a motivational one-liner. What goes wrong is the wording, the missing source, and a near-twin credited to somebody else entirely.

items.why: Quotation collections routinely print “Failure is an event, never a person” over the name William D. Brown, with no book or page attached. Full-text search finds that wording in anthologies crediting him and in Ziglar’s own books ↗ — it runs “failure is an event, never a person; an attitude, not an outcome” in You Can Reach the Top, What I Learned on the Way to the Top and Zig Ziglar’s Little Instruction Book — but never in a book Brown wrote. Brown’s Welcome Stress! was published in 1983 — after Ziglar’s book was already in print.

In the book the clause does not stand alone: it reads “failure is an event, it is not a person — yesterday ended last night,” as Wikiquote’s sourced entry records ↗. The share-card version keeps the slogan and drops the clause that explains it.

Aggregators carry “Remember that failure is an event, not a person” with no work named at all. That prefixed form is also authentically Ziglar’s — it turns up in Born to Win and Raising Positive Kids in a Negative World ↗ — but the quote sites cannot tell you that, because they never checked.

misattribution.truthLine: The thought and the words are both Ziglar’s. Wikiquote’s sourced section ↗ places the sentence in See You at the Top, citing the revised 2000 edition; the surrounding paragraph is present in the digitized Pelican printings ↗ of the book.

context.heading: Why the sentence was built this way
lead: Ziglar spent his career selling to people who had just been told no, and the line does a very specific job: it moves “failure” out of the identity column and into the events column. In the See You at the Top text Wikiquote quotes — the revised 2000 edition — it arrives at the end of a paragraph about put-downs, the argument being that a person who does something bad is not the same thing as a bad person. The failure sentence is the punchline of that argument, not a standalone aphorism.

That is also why the tail matters. In the book the clause is followed immediately by “yesterday ended last night,” which supplies the reason the first half is true: an event is bounded in time, and a person is not. Strip the tail, as most quote cards do, and you keep the slogan but lose the argument.
context.detailsSummary: The book had a different title first
detailsBody: Ziglar’s debut was issued as Biscuits, Fleas, and Pump Handles before being retitled; library catalog records for the Pelican printings still carry the double title — See you at the top = formerly entitled Biscuits, fleas, and pump handles ↗.

He kept reusing the line for the rest of his life. Full-text search turns it up in Raising Positive Kids in a Negative World, Something Else to Smile About, You Can Reach the Top, Success for Dummies, Zig Ziglar’s Little Instruction Book and Born to Win — sometimes as “failure is an event, not a person,” sometimes with the “Remember that…” prefix that quote sites now print.

sourcesVerified.claim: Wikiquote's sourced section for Zig Ziglar places "failure is an event, it is not a person — yesterday ended last night" in See You at the Top under the section heading "See You at the Top (2000)" — the revised 25th-anniversary edition, not the 1970s text — and lists "Failure is an event, not a person. Yesterday ended last night." as a variant. It also gives his dates as November 6, 1926 – November 28, 2012.

The Internet Archive holds a scanned Pelican Publishing printing of See You at the Top dated 1979, catalogued as "See you at the top = formerly entitled Biscuits, fleas, and pump handles" by Zig Ziglar.

Full-text search of scanned books returns the sentence "...is a vast difference between a 'bad' person and a person who does something bad" inside three digitized editions of Zig Ziglar's See You at the Top.

The exact wording "failure is an event, not a person" appears inside books authored by Zig Ziglar, including Success for Dummies, You Can Reach the Top, Born to Win, Inspiration: 365 Days a Year and Zig Ziglar's Little Instruction Book.
The prefixed form "Remember that failure is an event, not a person" appears inside Ziglar's own Born to Win and Raising Positive Kids in a Negative World.

The variant "failure is an event, never a person" appears inside anthologies and other authors' books that credit it to William D. Brown, and also inside Ziglar's own You Can Reach the Top, What I Learned on the Way to the Top and Zig Ziglar's Little Instruction Book (as "failure is an event, never a person; an attitude, not an outcome"). It appears in no book written by Brown himself.
Goodreads carries "Failure is an event, never a person." credited to William D. Brown with no source book named.
William D. Brown's book Welcome Stress! was published in 1983 by CompCare Publications.

Wikipedia gives Zig Ziglar's dates as November 6, 1926 – November 28, 2012, his birthplace as Coffee County, Alabama, his 1947 start as a WearEver Cookware salesman, the 1977 founding of Ziglar, Inc., and lists See You at the Top as published in 1975 by Pelican.
Quote Investigator has no article on "failure is an event" — a site search returns no results.
Goodreads' See You at the Top quote listing carries the wording "failure is an event, it is not a person—yesterday ended last night—today is a brand new day and it's yours" attributed to the book.
Ziglar Inc.'s official quotes site restates that "failure is an event, not a person" reflects Ziglar's position on failure.
